original_metadata.title: Two one-sided tests for average bioequivalence: a worked example with simulated data

document_metadata.title: Two one-sided tests for average bioequivalence: a worked example with simulated data
document_metadata.abstract: Average bioequivalence is usually shown with the two one-sided tests procedure (TOST). We explain the procedure with a simulated crossover study of a fictional generic formulation and show that it is equivalent to checking whether the 90% confidence interval of the geometric mean ratio lies within 80 to 125 percent.

elements.text: A generic formulation may replace the reference product when both lead to the same systemic exposure. Classical significance tests are not suitable for this question, because a non-significant difference does not prove equivalence. The two one-sided tests procedure reverses the hypotheses: the null hypothesis states that the formulations differ by more than an acceptable margin.

We simulated a two-period, two-sequence crossover study with 24 healthy volunteers. The area under the curve and the peak concentration were log-transformed and analysed with a linear mixed model containing sequence, period and formulation as fixed effects and subject as random effect. Each of the two one-sided tests was carried out at a significance level of five percent. The test product is declared bioequivalent if both tests reject, which is the same as requiring the 90% confidence interval of the geometric mean ratio to lie completely within the acceptance range of 80 to 125 percent.

The geometric mean ratio of the area under the curve was 0.97 with a 90% confidence interval from 0.91 to 1.04. For the peak concentration the ratio was 1.05 and the interval ranged from 0.96 to 1.15. Both one-sided tests rejected for both parameters, so the fictional generic formulation would be considered bioequivalent. The within-subject coefficient of variation was 14 percent.

The worked example reproduces the textbook result that TOST at five percent and the 90% confidence interval approach lead to the same decision. For highly variable drugs a reference-scaled approach widens the acceptance range, and the sample size has to be planned for the expected variability and the true ratio.
